title: Pause: Christmas
tagline: Making a screen-time app feel like Christmas, without making it feel too childish.
headline: How do you make Christmas feel grown up?
summary: Pause's Christmas theme, from moodboard to App Store in about two weeks: hand-pressed clay, one garland lit for day and night, carved type, a new puzzle, and a free December.
outcomes: 8 design rounds, from candy clay to carved-in-sand
74 screens rebuilt from one set of rules
Premium free all December. Results in January
lessons: Say what you don't want, not just what you do
Pull the look apart, then keep the best of each round
Make the last call by hand, then let Claude spread it
A theme is a product decision too
article:
Every season I give Pause a new look. Halloween got something spooky, Thanksgiving got something cozy (and a new Gratitude puzzle), and then Christmas came along and felt like the big one. The tricky part was the brief I gave myself: make the app feel like Christmas, and a little playful, without it feeling too childish. Pause is for grown-ups who are trying to take their time back from their phones, and I didn't want to hand them something that looks like a kids' app.

I also had a hard deadline. The theme had to be in the App Store by December 1, so I had about two weeks to design it, build it, and get it approved. I designed it in Figma and built it with Claude Code, same as the rest of Pause. This world is how it went, step by step, including the parts I got wrong.

**Tools:** Figma, Claude Code, SwiftUI, PostHog, Applyra

![The moodboard I started from, with a note on every reference](content/pause-christmas/moodboard.jpg)

## 1. A moodboard, with a "not this"

Before I made a single screen, I put together a moodboard. Clay icons, 3D clay illustrations, buttons and cards that look like Play-Doh, and a Santa Tracker page I liked as a reference for dark mode. I wrote a little note on every one saying why I liked it. "I like these clayish icons." "This is good for a dark theme." And on one of them I wrote "this feels too child oriented."

That last note ended up being the most useful one. It told Claude what to stay away from, not just what to copy, and I kept coming back to it in every round after. I also couldn't find a Christmas app I actually liked, so I couldn't borrow the colors from anywhere. I knew I wanted whites, yellows, browns and reds, and I had to figure out the rest on my own.

## 2. Keep the clay, change the mood

My first round was candy-bright clay, with snow, butter, gingerbread, cranberry and pine, round friendly headings and puffy shadows. I really liked the texture of the clay buttons, but the whole thing felt a little childish. So instead of throwing the round away, I split it into two things: the material, which was clay, and the mood, which was too young.

I kept the clay and changed everything around it. Deeper colors like oxblood, antique gold and ivory, quieter shapes, and a script font, but only for big one-word moments. The script never goes on buttons or body text, so everything stays easy to read.

## 3. One garland, lit for night

At first, light mode and dark mode had different decorations, mistletoe in the day and a string of Christmas lights at night. I didn't like how the lights turned out. So I asked for the same garland in both, just lit differently for the dark side, white and gold and a little shiny. Same decoration, two moods, and it feels like one app instead of two.

I also kept an eye on how heavy each color felt. Red is saved for the main button and the ornaments, and the big Your Week card went calm.

![The Dashboard in light and midnight: one garland, lit two ways](content/pause-christmas/dashboards.jpg)

## 4. Colors you can tell apart

When I designed the Thanksgiving theme, a lot of people told me the fruit colors were too similar, and it made the puzzle harder to solve. Fair enough, honestly. So for Christmas I made the ornaments as different from each other as I could, and I added red and green velvet bands to some of them, so even when two are the same color, or close, you can still tell them apart.

![Ball Sort in light and midnight](content/pause-christmas/ballsort-screens.jpg)

## 5. Clay you can feel

The first version looked like clay, but it didn't feel like clay. When you actually play with it, nothing is perfectly smooth. The edges are uneven and you can see where your thumb pressed. So every card and button got a wobbly, hand-made edge, no two the same, and a fine grain like sand.

I tuned the grain myself in Figma's noise settings until it looked right, and then Claude copied it across about 70 elements. That's kind of how we worked the whole time. I made the call on the look by hand, and Claude spread it everywhere else.

![v5: sandy clay and rough snow hills](content/pause-christmas/v5.jpg)

## 6. A detour on purpose

I liked where the clay was heading, but I had a worry in the back of my head that it might feel too juvenile for the people who actually use Pause. So before I committed, I asked for the opposite on purpose: a calm, grown-up version made of paper and velvet, with thin crisp lines and soft shadows.

When I saw it, it felt way too modern. But putting the two next to each other made the trade-off easy to see, which is the whole reason to do it. I kept a few of the paper version's ideas, like how the cards sit, and went back to the clay for the rest.

![v7: the paper and velvet detour, side by side with clay](content/pause-christmas/v7.jpg)

## 7. Carved in sand

After a while, the script font and the fancy serif started to feel like they came from a different world than the handmade clay. I still wanted a serif, just one that belonged with the material. So I asked for titles that look carved into the page, like someone wrote with a finger in the sand.

Claude built the carving out of light instead of a filter, with a shadow along the top edge of each letter and a little lit lip underneath. We tried a few fonts side by side, and I picked DM Serif Display, which wasn't the one Claude recommended. The carving is what makes it look handmade, and its sharper lines keep everything feeling grown up.

![Carved in sand: Fraunces vs DM Serif Display](content/pause-christmas/carved.jpg)

## 8. 74 screens, one set of rules

Once I knew the look, we rebuilt all 37 screens, in light and midnight, so 74 in total, in one pass. Instead of fixing screens one by one, we wrote the rules once: which font goes where, which colors swap for which, every card and button turned into clay, and the garland placed under each screen's first line. When something broke, we fixed the rule and not the screen, which saved me a ton of time.

The puzzle thumbnails, memory cards, app icon, App Store screenshots and the website followed the same rules, so the marketing can't drift away from the app.

![The puzzle thumbnails in light and midnight](content/pause-christmas/thumbs.jpg)

## 9. A new puzzle for December: Santa's Traffic

December also got a brand new puzzle. You slide clay cars and trucks along their lanes to clear the road so Santa's car can get out. Santa's convertible is the only red piece on the board, so you always know which one to free. There are 60 boards, so it should keep people busy for a while.

![Santa's car and the clay traffic](content/pause-christmas/santa.jpg)

## 10. Free all December

The biggest decision wasn't really about how it looks. For the whole month of December, Pause Premium is free for everybody. Every puzzle, as many apps as you want, no ads, no card, and nothing to cancel.

The idea is simple. I'd love for people to spend more time with the people they love over the holidays, and less time on their phones. With everything unlocked, you get to feel what it's really like to use social media on purpose, not a watered-down version of it. On January 1 it ends on its own, and you'll see a one-time New Year screen with the plans, and the free plan is still there. I looked at Apple's offer codes and a month-long free trial, but a simple date switch inside the app was the only way to make it truly free without needing anything from Apple.

![Premium is free all December](content/pause-christmas/store-free.jpg)

## 11. What I'm measuring

The theme goes live on December 1, so I don't have results yet, and I'd rather tell you that than make something up. I'm going to share the free month everywhere I can. What I'm watching is how many people it brings in, and how many of them stick around after Christmas, whether that means they're still using Pause in January or they pick a plan.

I'm also curious whether more reviews and messages come in, and what people say. And since Pause is connected to PostHog, I'll be able to see how people actually use it when nothing is locked: how many apps they pause, which puzzles they pick, and how often they unlock. I'll come back and update this page in January with the real numbers.

## What I learned

Tell the tools what you don't want, and not just what you do. One "not this" on my moodboard helped me more than any of the references. Pull the look apart into pieces too, the material, the mood, the type, the decorations, and judge each one on its own, because then you can keep the best part of every round.

And make the last call by hand, then let Claude spread it everywhere else. Oh, and a theme is a product decision too. Honestly, the free month matters more than the garland, haha.
